text: By eighteen twelve, Napoleon Bonaparte ran most of Europe.
Russia's new tsar, Alexander the First, stopped playing by Napoleon's rules. So Napoleon invaded, with the biggest army Europe had ever seen: around six hundred thousand men.
[whistling] That's not an army. That's a country on a walking holiday.
And the Russians did something infuriating. They kept retreating. And as they went, they burned their own crops and villages, so the French found nothing to eat.
When the Russians finally stood and fought, at Borodino, around seventy thousand men were killed or wounded in a single day.
Then the Russians pulled back again... and Napoleon marched into Moscow.
He expected the tsar to beg for peace. Instead, he found an almost empty city. And that night, fires broke out everywhere. Most of Moscow burned.
[impatient] Has the tsar answered?
No, sire.
Then send him another letter. A nicer one.
[reading] Sire, this one has a little drawing of us shaking hands.
[pause] ...Add a heart.
Alexander never answered. After five weeks in a burned city, Napoleon gave up and turned for home.
And then came Russia's oldest ally: winter.
Starving, freezing soldiers collapsed in the snow, while Cossacks picked off anyone who fell behind. Only a small fraction of that giant army made it out.
[shivering] Rule number one of invading Russia: don't.
The Russians chased Napoleon across Europe, and in eighteen fourteen, Russian soldiers paraded through Paris.
But those officers had seen something in the West. Constitutions. Laws that even kings had to follow.
In December eighteen twenty-five, a group of them marched their troops into a square in Saint Petersburg to demand change. The Decembrists.
The new tsar, Nicholas the First, answered with cannons. Five leaders were hanged. Over a hundred were sent to Siberia.
Then Russia lost the Crimean War, on its own doorstep, against Britain, France and the Ottomans.
That shock finally forced change. In eighteen sixty-one, Alexander the Second freed around twenty-three million serfs. Two years before Abraham Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation.

And Russia needed money. It couldn't really defend a faraway colony across the ocean anyway. So in eighteen sixty-seven, Alexander sold Alaska to the United States for seven point two million dollars.
[tapping his watch, grinning] And there it is. The garage sale from the start of the video.
Some Americans laughed and called it Seward's Folly, after the man who bought it. Then came the gold. Then the oil. Nobody's laughing now.
Alexander reformed the courts, the army, local government. And on March the thirteenth, eighteen eighty-one, he approved a plan that could have been Russia's first step towards an elected assembly.
That same afternoon, revolutionaries threw a bomb at his carriage. It missed. Alexander stepped out to check on the wounded... and a second bomber threw another, right at his feet.
[quietly] The tsar who freed the serfs. Killed the day he tried to give people a voice.
His son tore up the plan. The loop was back on its old setting. And the tsar after that... would be the last one.
